question.prompt:
The figure below shows line \(\ell\) with a regular, infinite, recurring pattern of squares and line segments.

[Figure 1](figures/2019_AMC_12A_Q06_question_fig1.svg)

How many of the following four kinds of rigid motion transformations of the plane in which this figure is drawn, other than the identity transformation, will transform this figure into itself?

• some rotation around a point of line \(\ell\)

• some translation in the direction parallel to line \(\ell\)

• the reflection across line \(\ell\)

• some reflection across a line perpendicular to line \(\ell\)

solutions.explanation:
View \(\ell\) as horizontal. The squares alternate above and below it, while every short slanted segment rises to the right. A motion must preserve both the squares and these attachments.

A nonidentity rotation works. Choose the point where \(\ell\) meets the right edge of an upper square. A \(180^\circ\) rotation about this point sends that square to the lower square immediately to its right. Its upper-right attachment becomes the lower-left attachment of that lower square. The same correspondence continues throughout the repeating pattern, so the whole figure is preserved.

A nonzero translation parallel to \(\ell\) also works. Translate by one full repeat, from an upper square to the next upper square. Every square and every attached segment then coincides with its next copy.

Reflection across \(\ell\) does not work: a segment that rises to the right would become one that falls to the right. No such slanted segments occur in the original pattern. Reflection across any line perpendicular to \(\ell\) also reverses the slant in this way, so none of those reflections works.

Exactly two of the four kinds of motion preserve the figure. The answer is \(\boxed{2}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
solutions.title: Track the squares and their attachments
